workers.title: Getting Started
workers.description: Scaffold the Bookmark API project, understand the Workers runtime, and test your first Worker locally.
objectives: Scaffold a Workers project and understand the generated file structure
Explain how the fetch handler receives and responds to HTTP requests
Use Wrangler to run, test, and iterate on a Worker locally

blocks.html: Before diving in, watch this overview of Workers architecture and concepts.

items.label: What we're building
items.html: A verified connection between your local machine and your Cloudflare account.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: Later steps create KV namespaces, D1 databases, and deploy your Worker. All of these require authentication. Setting this up first prevents confusing errors later.

blocks.code:
# Log in to your Cloudflare account (opens a browser window)
npx wrangler login

# Verify you are authenticated
npx wrangler whoami

blocks.html: You should see your account name and ID. If not, run npx wrangler login again.

blocks.title: Don't Skip This
blocks.html: If you skip authentication, commands like npx wrangler kv namespace create, npx wrangler d1 create, and npx wrangler deploy will fail with auth errors in later steps.

blocks.text: Step 2: Create the Bookmark API Project

items.label: What we're building
items.html: A new Cloudflare Worker project called bookmark-api running locally.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: Every Workers project starts with a scaffold. This gives you the project structure, TypeScript config, and local dev server.

blocks.code:
# Create the project
npm create cloudflare@latest -- bookmark-api --type hello-world --ts

# Navigate into the project
cd bookmark-api

# Start the local dev server
npm run dev

blocks.html: Running npm create cloudflare@latest will trigger a series of interactive prompts (e.g. package manager, git initialization, deploy). Accept the defaults for each prompt to match the configuration used throughout this workshop.

  • wrangler.jsonc - Wrangler CLI configuration (name, entry point, bindings)

  • tsconfig.json - TypeScript configuration

workers.title: Persistent Storage with KV
workers.description: Replace the in-memory bookmark store with Workers KV so bookmarks persist across restarts and deployments.
objectives: Connect an external resource to a Worker using bindings
Swap an in-memory data layer for persistent KV storage without changing the API contract
Reason about eventual consistency and when KV is the right storage choice

blocks.title: What Changes in This Step
blocks.html: Your Bookmark API works, but bookmarks are lost whenever the Worker restarts. In this step you will create a Workers KV namespace and replace the in-memory Map with KV operations. The API endpoints and response format stay exactly the same. Only the storage layer changes.

items.label: What we're building
items.html: A KV namespace called BOOKMARKS bound to your Worker.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: KV provides globally distributed, persistent key-value storage that survives Worker restarts and deployments.

blocks.code: npx wrangler kv namespace create "BOOKMARKS"

blocks.html: When prompted “Would you like Wrangler to add it on your behalf?”, type Y. This adds the KV binding to your wrangler.jsonc.
Then regenerate your types so TypeScript knows about the binding:

blocks.code: npx wrangler types

blocks.title: What Is a Binding?
blocks.html: A binding connects an external resource (KV, D1, R2, AI) to your Worker. After binding, the resource is available on the env object, e.g. env.BOOKMARKS. No API keys or connection strings needed.

blocks.text: Step 2: Update the Handlers to Use KV

items.label: What we're building
items.html: All four CRUD handlers using KV instead of the in-memory Map.

items.label: Why this matters

blocks.title: N+1 Query Pattern
blocks.html: The listBookmarks function calls .list() once and then .get() for every key. This is called the N+1 pattern and it works fine for a small number of bookmarks, but gets slow as the dataset grows. The challenge at the end of this step shows how to avoid this using KV metadata. Also note that .list() returns at most 1,000 keys per call. For larger datasets, you would need to paginate using the cursor returned in the response.

items.html: Bookmarks that survive a Worker restart.

items.label: Why this matters

blocks.title: Eventual Consistency
blocks.html:
KV is eventually consistent. In production, a write may take up to 60 seconds to propagate to all 300+ data centers. Reads from the same location that wrote the data are immediate. In local development with Wrangler, all reads and writes are immediate.
This makes KV ideal for data that is read frequently and written infrequently (configuration, bookmarks, feature flags). For data that requires strong consistency, you will use D1 in the next step.

blocks.title: Try It Yourself
blocks.html:
1. Add expiring bookmarks: Use KV’s expirationTtl option to create bookmarks that auto-delete after a set time. Hint: env.BOOKMARKS.put(id, data, { expirationTtl: 3600 }) sets a 1-hour TTL.
  2. Add metadata: KV supports storing metadata alongside values. Store the bookmark’s title as KV metadata so you can list bookmarks without fetching each value individually. Hint: env.BOOKMARKS.put(id, data, { metadata: { title } }) and keys.keys[i].metadata.

workers.title: D1 Database with KV Caching
workers.description: Migrate bookmarks to a D1 SQL database for relational queries and tags, while keeping KV as a read cache for fast lookups.
objectives: Define a SQL schema and apply migrations with D1
Implement the cache-aside pattern with D1 as the source of truth and KV as a read cache
Decide when to use relational storage vs key-value storage in the same application

blocks.title: What Changes in This Step
blocks.html: KV is great for simple key-value lookups, but bookmarks need relational features: filtering by tag, sorting by date, searching by title. D1 provides SQL for this. You will migrate the primary storage to D1 and keep KV as a read cache. When a bookmark is requested by ID, the Worker checks KV first and falls back to D1. This pattern (cache-aside) is common in production applications.

items.label: What we're building
items.html: A D1 database bound to your Worker alongside the existing KV namespace.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: D1 gives you SQL queries, joins, and filtering that KV cannot provide.

blocks.code: npx wrangler d1 create bookmark-db

blocks.html: When prompted “Would you like Wrangler to add it on your behalf?”, type Y. Wrangler will then ask for a binding name. Enter DB so it matches the env.DB calls used throughout this workshop.
Regenerate types:

blocks.code: npx wrangler types

items.label: What we're building
items.html: A bookmarks table with columns for URL, title, tags, and timestamps.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: A well-designed schema is the foundation of your relational data layer.

blocks.html: Create schema.sql in your project root:

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS bookmarks (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  url TEXT NOT NULL,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  tags TEXT DEFAULT '',
  created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

blocks.title: Re-running the Schema
blocks.html: We use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS so you can safely re-run this file without losing data. If you need to reset the table during development, you can manually run DROP TABLE bookmarks; first, but be aware this deletes all existing bookmarks.
Apply it to the local database. Make sure the dev server is stopped before running this:

blocks.code: npx wrangler d1 execute bookmark-db --local --file=./schema.sql

blocks.title: no such table: bookmarks
blocks.html: If you see this error when testing, the migration above was not applied. Re-run the command and restart the dev server with npm run dev.

items.label: What we're building
items.html: Handlers that use D1 as the source of truth and KV as a read cache.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: This demonstrates a real-world caching pattern: write to D1, cache in KV, read from KV first.

blocks.html: Replace src/index.ts with the following. Key changes from Step 3 are marked:

blocks.title: Cache-Aside Pattern
blocks.html:
This code implements the cache-aside (lazy-loading) pattern:
  1. Read: Check KV first. On cache miss, query D1 and populate KV.
  2. Write: Write to D1, then write to KV (write-through).
  3. Delete: Delete from D1, then delete from KV (cache invalidation).
The _cached: true field in the response lets you verify caching is working during testing.

items.label: What we're building
items.html: Bookmarks stored in D1 with KV caching verified.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: Testing confirms the migration is complete and both storage layers work together.

blocks.title: When to Use KV vs D1
blocks.html:
You are now using both in the same Worker:
This is a common production pattern. KV handles the hot path (individual bookmark lookups) while D1 handles queries that need SQL (filtering by tag, listing with pagination).

workers.title: AI-Powered Summaries
workers.description: Add Workers AI to automatically generate a summary for each bookmark when it is saved, storing the result in D1.
objectives: Integrate a text generation model into an existing data pipeline
Design AI calls that fail gracefully without blocking core operations
Evaluate when to run inference inline vs as a background task

blocks.title: What Changes in This Step
blocks.html: When a user creates a bookmark, the API will now call Workers AI to generate a one-sentence summary of the URL based on its title. The summary is stored in D1 alongside the bookmark. If the AI call fails, the bookmark is still saved. The summary is a nice-to-have, not a blocker.

blocks.title: Workers AI Requires --remote
blocks.html:
Workers AI models run on Cloudflare’s network, not locally. To test AI features during development, start the dev server with the --remote flag:
Without --remote, AI calls will fail or return empty results. The --remote flag runs your Worker locally but executes binding calls (AI, KV, D1) against your real Cloudflare account. You must be logged in (npx wrangler whoami) for this to work.

blocks.code: npx wrangler dev --remote

This workshop uses @cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct-fast, a good balance of quality and speed. Workers AI offers many models for different tasks:

workers.title: AI Gateway
workers.description: Route your Workers AI calls through AI Gateway for caching, monitoring, and cost control. A small configuration change with big operational benefits.
objectives: Route AI inference through a managed gateway for observability and cost control
Choose cache TTLs based on response stability and freshness requirements
Interpret gateway analytics to identify optimization opportunities

blocks.title: What Changes in This Step
blocks.html: This is the smallest code change in the workshop. You will create an AI Gateway, add one environment variable, and pass a gateway option to each env.AI.run() call. Everything else stays the same. The payoff is significant: caching, analytics, rate limiting, and request logging for all your AI calls.

items.label: What we're building
items.html: An AI Gateway configured in the Cloudflare Dashboard.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: The gateway sits between your Worker and the AI models, providing observability and caching without changing your application logic.

items: Go to the Cloudflare Dashboard
Select AI > AI Gateway
Click Create Gateway
Name it bookmark-gateway and click Create

items.label: What we're building
items.html: All env.AI.run() calls routed through AI Gateway.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: Adding the gateway option enables caching, monitoring, and rate limiting for every AI request.

blocks.html: The change is small. In src/index.ts, update the generateSummary function that calls env.AI.run():
That is the entire code change. The rest of the file stays exactly the same.

blocks.title: Gateway Options
blocks.html:
The gateway option is the third argument to env.AI.run():
  • id: Your gateway name (must match what you created in the Dashboard)
  • skipCache: Set to true to bypass the cache for this specific request
  • cacheTtl: How long (in seconds) to cache the response
If two requests send the same prompt to the same model, the second request will be served from the gateway cache without consuming AI inference.

items.label: What we're building
items.html: Verified that duplicate AI requests are served from the gateway cache.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: Cache hits mean faster responses and lower costs.

blocks.code: npx wrangler dev --remote

blocks.title: Gateway Caching Requires --remote or Deployment
blocks.html: AI Gateway is a cloud service. When running locally without --remote, AI calls do not route through the gateway, so you will not see caching or analytics. Use --remote to test gateway features during development, or deploy with npx wrangler deploy and test against the live URL. The analytics dashboard (Step 4) only shows data from remote/deployed requests.

blocks.html: The second creation sends the same prompt to the AI model. Because the gateway caches by prompt, this request should return faster with a similar summary served from cache.

blocks.text: Step 4: View Analytics in the Dashboard

items.label: What we're building
items.html: An understanding of the metrics available in the AI Gateway Dashboard.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: Observability lets you optimize costs, debug issues, and understand usage patterns.

blocks.html: After deploying (npx wrangler deploy), go to AI > AI Gateway > bookmark-gateway in the Dashboard. You will see:

items: Request count - Total AI requests routed through the gateway
Cache hit rate - Percentage served from cache (your cost savings)
Latency - Average and p99 response times
Token usage - Input and output tokens consumed
Error rate - Failed AI requests

blocks.html: In the gateway settings, you can set request limits per minute to prevent runaway costs from unexpected traffic.

blocks.title: Cache TTL Strategy
blocks.html:
Choose cache durations based on how stable the content is:
  • Bookmark summaries (24h): Same title and URL always produce a similar summary
  • Chat-style responses (skip or 5 min): Users expect dynamic responses

blocks.title: Try It Yourself
blocks.html:
1. Compare response times: Create the same bookmark twice (delete and recreate) and use curl -w "\nTime: %{time_total}s\n" to compare the response time of the first request (fresh inference) vs the second request (gateway cache hit). How much faster is the cached response?
  2. Experiment with cache TTL: Try changing the cacheTtl value in generateSummary and observe how it affects cache behavior in the gateway dashboard.

workers.title: Deploy to Production
workers.description: Deploy your Bookmark API to Cloudflare's global network, verify the deployment, and learn how to monitor and roll back.
objectives: Ship a Worker to Cloudflare's global network and verify it is live
Store sensitive configuration securely using Wrangler secrets
Monitor production traffic and roll back a bad deployment

items.label: What we're building
items.html: Your D1 database schema applied to the remote (production) database.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: In Step 4 you ran the schema migration with --local, which only writes to a local SQLite file. The remote database needs the base schema before deploying.

blocks.html: First, verify you are authenticated:

blocks.code: npx wrangler whoami

blocks.html: Apply the base schema to the remote D1 database. The summary column migration was already applied remotely in Step 5, so you only need the initial schema:

blocks.code: npx wrangler d1 execute bookmark-db --remote --file=./schema.sql

blocks.title: Why Is This Needed?
blocks.html: In Step 4, the d1 execute command used --local, which writes to a local SQLite file. The remote D1 database does not have the bookmarks table yet. Skipping this step is the most common cause of “table not found” errors after first deploy.

blocks.title: Security: AI-Generated Code is Untrusted Code
blocks.html:
Even with good prompting, LLMs can produce unexpected or malicious code. The sandbox protects you from the worst outcomes, but you should also:

blocks.title: Building Live Development Environments
blocks.html:
The sandbox can run entire applications, not just snippets. Use it to build:
  • PR previews — spin up a full app for every pull request
  • AI-generated app previews — let users see their generated app running live
  • Interactive tutorials — give learners a real running environment
  • Coding playgrounds — safe, shareable live demos
Key APIs for this:
  • gitCheckout() — clone a repo into /workspace
  • startProcess() — start a long-running dev server (non-blocking)
  • exposePort() — make a container port accessible via URL
  • proxyToSandbox() — route incoming Worker requests to the container

In this step, you’ll build a single POST /preview endpoint that clones a repository, installs dependencies, starts a dev server, and returns a live preview URL. You’ll add each piece incrementally — testing as you go — so you can see the endpoint grow from a simple clone into a full preview pipeline.

blocks.title: Process Readiness Methods
blocks.html:
The Process object returned by startProcess() has built-in methods to wait until the process is actually ready:
  • process.waitForPort(port) — waits until the process is listening on a port (HTTP or TCP check)
  • process.waitForLog(pattern) — waits until a string or RegExp appears in the process output
  • process.waitForExit() — waits until the process terminates and returns the exit code
All three accept an optional timeout in milliseconds. Always prefer these over setTimeout() — they’re faster (no wasted time) and more reliable (no missed startup delays).

blocks.title: How proxyToSandbox() Works
blocks.html:
When a request arrives at your Worker, proxyToSandbox() checks if it matches a proxied sandbox port. If it does, the request is forwarded to the container and the response is returned transparently — your Worker acts as a reverse proxy.
This means your app and all its assets (JS, CSS, images) are served through the same Worker URL.

For local development this doesn’t matter — localhost works fine. For production, you’ll need to set up a custom domain with wildcard DNS routing. See the Production Deployment guide for setup instructions.

blocks.title: Security is Your Responsibility
blocks.html:
The Sandbox SDK provides strong container-level isolation, but it doesn’t automatically protect you from every threat. When running AI-generated or user-provided code, you must:
  • Validate all inputs before they touch the sandbox
  • Isolate users so they can’t see each other’s data
  • Never pass real secrets into the sandbox environment
  • Log everything so you can audit what ran
The sandbox can’t be exploited to break out to your host — but it can still be misused if you don’t apply these patterns.

blocks.title: What Sandbox IDs Guarantee
blocks.html:
Two sandboxes with different IDs have completely separate:
  • File systems (/workspace contents)
  • Running processes
  • Environment variables set via setEnvVars()
  • Memory and CPU usage
They share: network access to the internet (both can make outbound requests).

items.label: What we're building
items.html: Secure patterns for passing configuration into sandbox commands at the right scope.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: Scoping env vars to the narrowest context — per-command or per-session — reduces the risk of leaking config across unrelated executions.

blocks.html: Per-command: scoped to a single exec() or startProcess() call
Per-context: scoped to a createCodeContext() for runCode() calls
Session-level: shared across a group of related commands

items.label: What we're building
items.html: A pattern where secrets stay in your Worker and are never exposed to sandbox code.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: AI-generated or user-supplied code could read environment variables and exfiltrate secrets to an external server.

blocks.html: Never pass real secrets to the sandbox:

Instead, proxy API calls through your Worker. In this pattern, code running inside the sandbox calls your Worker’s proxy endpoint (e.g., fetch("https://your-worker.dev/proxy/stripe", ...)). The Worker validates the request, attaches authentication using secrets that never leave the Worker, and forwards it to the external API:

items.label: What we're building
items.html: A complete authentication flow that gates sandbox access to verified users.

items.label: Why this matters
items.html: Without authentication, anyone who discovers your Worker URL can execute arbitrary code in your sandboxes.

items.label: What we're building

blocks.title: setKeepAlive() vs sleepAfter
blocks.html:
setKeepAlive(true) prevents automatic sleep entirely by sending heartbeat pings every 30 seconds — use it when you need the sandbox to stay alive during long operations.
For controlling how long a sandbox waits before sleeping, use the sleepAfter option when creating the sandbox:
Always call setKeepAlive(false) or destroy() when done — containers with keepAlive enabled will not automatically timeout and will count toward your account limits.

items: Go to Workers & Pages → your worker
Click Logs to see real-time invocation logs
Check Metrics for request counts, error rates, and CPU time
Open Settings → Observability to configure log retention
